title: Shared Responsibility in Azure & GCP 🌐
description: How Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud define their boundaries.

slides.title: Azure: "Security of the Platform" vs "Security on the Platform" 🛡️
slides.content:
## Microsoft's Take

Azure's model is identical in spirit:
- **Microsoft responsibility (security OF the platform)**: Physical hosts, network, data centres, and the hypervisor.
- **Customer responsibility (security ON the platform)**: Guest OS, applications, data, endpoints, accounts, and access management.
- **Nuance**: For managed services like Azure SQL Database, the boundary shifts – Microsoft handles OS and engine patches.

*Same song, different singer.*

quizData.question: For an Azure Virtual Machine, who is responsible for encrypting the OS disk at rest?

options.text: The customer must enable and manage encryption
No one – Azure VMs are unencrypted by design

quizData.explanation: Azure may offer default encryption for managed disks, but the customer is responsible for key management and verifying encryption settings.

slides.title: Azure Shared Responsibility by Service Type 📋
slides.content:
| Scenario | Microsoft | Customer |
|----------|-----------|----------|
| On‑premises data centre | Nothing | Everything |
| IaaS (Virtual Machines) | Physical infra, hypervisor | OS, apps, NSG, data |
| PaaS (Azure App Service) | OS, runtime, platform | App code, data, identity |
| SaaS (Microsoft 365) | Application stack | Data classification, access governance |

*The pattern is clear: the higher you go, the less you touch.*

slides.title: GCP: "Security of the Cloud" & Beyond 🌩️
slides.content:
## Google's Approach

GCP uses the exact same terminology as AWS: "security of the cloud" (Google) vs "security in the cloud" (you).

- **Google manages**: Hardware, network, physical security, and the software stack for managed services.
- **You manage**: Your data, access policies, encryption keys (if using customer‑managed keys), and any application‑level security.
- **Differentiator**: GCP strongly promotes encryption by default – data at rest is encrypted automatically, but you control the keys if you wish. That doesn't absolve you from key management if you bring your own keys (CMEK).

quizData.question: In Google Cloud, all data at rest is automatically encrypted, so the customer has no responsibility for encryption.
quizData.explanation: GCP encrypts data at rest by default, but the customer is still responsible for managing access to that data and for any customer‑supplied encryption keys (CMEK).

slides.title: Compute Engine vs. Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) ⚙️
slides.content:
## Two Levels of Responsibility

- **Compute Engine (IaaS)**: You manage the VM, OS patches, and network tags (firewall). Google manages the physical host.
- **GKE Standard (shared)**: You manage worker nodes (if using standard cluster) and the container images. Google manages the control plane.
- **GKE Autopilot (PaaS‑ish)**: Google manages the nodes, OS, and control plane; you bring containers, network policies, and IAM.

*See how the responsibility shifts as the service becomes more managed?*

slides.title: Cross‑Provider Consistency 💡
slides.content:
## One Rule to Rule Them All
Regardless of provider, **identity and access management (IAM) is ALWAYS your responsibility**. No provider will configure who can access your resources – that's your job. Master IAM, and you master cloud security.
